description: baseline (new dev+test-holdout methodology): lora_train_generative.py as-is defaults (--lean-prompt --df-path emnllp-dialog-flow-dialog-flow.json, batch-size=1, epochs=3, lora_r=8 q_proj,v_proj, lr=2e-4, grad-accum=4), test-holdout=500 randomly split from train (split_seed=1667046644, disjoint from the 1853 trained on). Best dev at epoch 2/3 (0.754; ep1=0.667, ep3 collapses to 0.620, same overfit-after-peak instability as the old dev-only baseline). Test-holdout (same best-epoch2 checkpoint) mean=0.643, clearly below dev's 0.754 -- gap driven almost entirely by st1 (dev 0.909 vs test 0.682, a 0.227 gap) while st2/st3_family track dev closely (within ~0.02); st3 also drops some (0.501->0.407). This dev/test gap is exactly the generalization signal the holdout was added to catch -- dev alone would have reported this run as much stronger than it is.

exp1: prior dev-only track's adopted-as-default recipe (full attn+FFN target-modules q_proj,k_proj,v_proj,o_proj,gate_proj,up_proj,down_proj) + --eval-batch-size 16 + epochs 3->1, all changed at once vs baseline -- confounds recipe vs epoch-budget, not a clean ablation (test-holdout also drawn from a different random split_seed=565205964 than baseline's, so raw test-vs-test deltas across rows carry extra sampling noise beyond what dev-vs-dev deltas do). dev=0.665 is well below baseline's dev=0.754, but test=0.664 is actually slightly ABOVE baseline's test=0.643 -- and dev/test agree tightly here (0.665 vs 0.664, gap ~0) vs baseline's large dev/test gap (0.754 vs 0.643). Read as: this recipe generalizes better/more consistently than baseline, but 1 epoch alone underperforms baseline's epoch-2 peak on dev. Discarding as a direct baseline replacement (needs a matched-epoch-budget rerun to isolate the target-modules effect), but the dev/test agreement is a good sign for full-target-modules -- worth revisiting at matched epochs.

exp2: diagnostic anchor, NOT a recipe change -- baseline's exact recipe (default q_proj,v_proj target-modules) but epochs 3->2 (still matched to where baseline's own best epoch landed) + --eval-batch-size 16 (dev/test eval batching only, shouldn't touch training). Built to give exp3 (full target-modules at the same epochs=2) a fair same-budget comparison point, since exp1 changed 3 variables at once. Best dev at epoch 2 = 0.633, well below baseline's epoch-2 dev=0.754 despite a near-identical recipe -- the only other difference is split_seed=644291970 (fresh random 500 held out, so the actual 1853 training examples differ from baseline's run too, not just eval batching). This means run-to-run dev noise is now larger than in the old dev-only track (there the training set was always the full unsplit train.jsonl, identical every run) -- the rotating holdout adds training-data-composition variance on top of ordinary training stochasticity. Test=0.679 held up fine (even slightly above dev here), so no overfitting red flag, just noisier dev comparisons going forward -- lean on larger effect sizes and don't over-read small deltas between rows with different split_seeds.

exp3: full attn+FFN target-modules (q_proj,k_proj,v_proj,o_proj,gate_proj,up_proj,down_proj) at the SAME epochs=2 budget as exp2's anchor -- the clean, matched-budget test of whether the old dev-only track's big "win" from this recipe (0.658->0.745 dev-only) survives a fair comparison + a held-out check. It does not: dev=0.659 vs exp2's 0.633 (+0.026) and test=0.673 vs exp2's 0.679 (-0.006) -- both deltas are small fractions of the ~0.12 run-to-run noise floor established by exp1/exp2, i.e. indistinguishable from noise on this evidence. Meanwhile the cost is real and reproduces the old track's finding: ~29-30min/epoch here vs exp2's ~22min/epoch, ~32% more expensive for adapting 7 module types instead of 2. Discarding per program.md's simplicity criterion -- no measurable benefit, real added cost. The prior track's "big win" for full-target-modules looks like it was mostly noise (single dev-only run, no held-out check, no matched-epoch control). Reverting to default q_proj,v_proj as the standing recipe.

exp4: default q_proj,v_proj target-modules (reverted per exp3) + lora_r 8->16, lora_alpha 16->32 (same 2:1 alpha/r ratio, more capacity), matched epochs=2, split_seed=899262687. dev=0.669 vs exp2 anchor's 0.633 (+0.036), test=0.687 vs exp2's 0.679 (+0.008) -- both deltas small fractions of the ~0.12 noise floor, same story as exp3: not distinguishable from noise. Also notable: best-dev landed at epoch 1 here (0.669), not epoch 2 (which dropped to 0.635) -- another data point that the "best epoch" location itself varies run to run (seen ep1 in the old dev-only baseline, ep2 in this track's baseline, ep1 here), so epoch budget can't be tuned down further than 2 without risking missing the peak. No clear capacity win; discarding, staying at lora_r=8 (simpler, cheaper, same 601k trainable-param budget as the default that's actually been tested twice now).

exp5: pure replicate of baseline's exact recipe (default q_proj,v_proj, epochs=3, --eval-batch-size 16 harmless-speedup only) with a fresh random split_seed=993048745. This is the critical reproducibility check for the standing-best baseline row (dev=0.754/test=0.643): it does NOT reproduce -- dev best (epoch 1 this time, not epoch 2) = 0.538, a full 0.216 BELOW baseline's dev=0.754 on an identical recipe/epoch-budget, only the held-out 500 (and therefore the actual 1853 training examples) differing. Test=0.544, close to this run's own dev (gap only +0.006, no overfitting flag). Conclusion: the true run-to-run noise floor from the rotating split alone is much larger than the ~0.09-0.12 estimated from exp1-4 (all of which used epochs<=2, never epochs=3) -- baseline's 0.754 looks like a favorable/high-end draw, not a reliable estimate of this recipe's typical performance. Every dev/test number recorded so far should be read as one noisy sample, not a precise estimate; don't treat baseline's row as a fixed target to beat without accounting for this. Discarding as a comparison point (redundant with baseline), keeping as the noise-floor reference instead.

exp6: --pos-weight enabled (per-label inverse-train-frequency completion-token weighting, st3_loss_weight left at default 1.0 so this isolates pos-weight alone), matched epochs=2, df-fix from commit 4ea32fd baked in automatically via --df-path. split_seed=1745993959. Headline: insufficient_context (0.000 in ALL 13 prior epoch-evals across 5 experiments) scored 0.600 on DEV at epoch 2/2 -- the first time it has ever been non-zero. Does not hold up on test: test insufficient_context=0.000 despite 8 real positives being present in this run's held-out 500 (confirmed by recomputing the split) -- so the model caught none of them there. With only 7 dev / 8 test positives for this label, both numbers are extremely high-variance (a single flip swings F1 by ~0.2-0.5); read the dev win as directionally promising but NOT yet confirmed generalization, not as a settled result. st3_macro_f1 overall: dev=0.503/test=0.460, vs the no-pos-weight matched-epoch anchor (exp2: dev=0.455/test=0.504) -- a wash, within noise, no clear aggregate st3 win either way. undisclosed_advertising also unchanged (dev=0.181, test=0.256, in line with prior runs' 0.10-0.32 range, pos_weight=5.68 wasn't large enough to move it clearly). st1 came in high this run (dev=0.761) with st2 flat -- no evidence of the st1/st2-for-st3 tradeoff the weighting is meant to induce, everything moved within the established noise band except insufficient_context's dev breakout. Keeping --pos-weight enabled going forward (no clear harm, plausible-but-unconfirmed upside on the task's most broken class) but flagging that insufficient_context needs several more runs before its F1 can be trusted either way -- 8-15 total examples cannot give a stable macro-F1 reading regardless of method.

exp7: --pos-weight + --st3-loss-weight 2.0 combined (multiplicative, e.g. insufficient_context ends up at 50*2=100x, inadequate_disclosure at 2.82*2=5.64x), matched epochs=2, split_seed=2059373460. Worse than exp6 (pos-weight alone) across the board: st3 dev=0.343/test=0.369 vs exp6's 0.503/0.460, st3_family dev=0.605/test=0.615 vs exp6's 0.665/0.704, and mean_macro_f1 dropped too (dev=0.563 vs exp6's 0.638). insufficient_context stayed at 0.000 in both epochs and test this time (didn't repeat exp6's dev=0.600 breakout even with 2x more weight on it). inadequate_disclosure -- a label that's never been badly broken (26%% of train, historically 0.34-0.68 F1) -- cratered to 0.000/0.124/0.250 across epoch1/epoch2/test, its worst showing in any experiment so far. Reads as over-weighting: stacking a flat 2x on top of pos_weight's already-large per-label multipliers pushes several labels' loss contribution too high relative to the rest of the field, destabilizing st3 calibration generally rather than helping the rare tail. Discarding the stack; reverting to pos-weight alone (st3-loss-weight=1.0, exp6's config) as the standing st3-focused recipe. Given insufficient_context's dev win in exp6 didn't repeat here either, it still needs more evidence either way -- next step should be repeat runs of exp6's exact config on fresh splits, not more aggressive weighting.

exp8: repeat of exp6's exact config (--pos-weight alone, st3-loss-weight=1.0, epochs=2) on a fresh split_seed=969090474, to check whether exp6's insufficient_context dev breakout (0.000->0.600) was a real effect or noise. It did not repeat: insufficient_context =0.000 in both epochs and on test here, same as every pre-exp6 run. Two repeats of the identical config now span dev st3=0.503 (exp6) vs 0.360 (this run) -- a 0.14 spread on identical hyperparameters, and neither clearly beats the no-pos-weight anchor (exp2: dev st3=0.455). undisclosed_advertising also unremarkable here (dev=0.197, test=0.266, within the historical 0.10-0.32 range). Conclusion: after 3 total pos-weight runs (exp6/7/8), --pos-weight's effect on st3 is NOT distinguishable from the established ~0.2 noise floor -- exp6's breakout looks like it was a favorable-noise draw (7 dev positives is too few to trust any single run's F1 on this label), not a reproducible win. Discarding as a proven improvement, though keeping --pos-weight enabled by default is still reasonable (no evidence of harm, some chance of real but small benefit that this sample size can't resolve). Further single-run hyperparameter pushes on this eval surface (500 test / 504 dev, several st3 labels under 3%% frequency) are unlikely to produce a distinguishable signal without a fundamentally different approach (e.g. averaging several repeat runs per config, or a much larger eval set).

exp9: --pos-weight + --oversample-rare-st3 5 (duplicates train instances containing insufficient_context/hfss_food_marketing/age_restricted_or_prohibited_product 5x, train 1853->2197), matched epochs=2, split_seed=735918932. Same pattern as exp7 (stacking a second st3-emphasis intervention on top of pos-weight alone): worse across the board, not better. st3 dev=0.335/test=0.324 vs exp6's (pos-weight alone) 0.503/0.460; st3_family dev=0.532/test=0.510 vs exp6's 0.665/0.704 -- 'disclosure' family specifically cratered (0.286/0.298/0.269 across epoch1/epoch2/test, its worst showing yet) and undisclosed_advertising hit new lows (0.000/0.054/0.110). insufficient_context: 0.000 (epoch1, the selected-best epoch)/0.250 (epoch2, not selected)/0.000 (test) -- a flicker of nonzero signal at epoch2 but not enough to call it working. This is the SECOND time stacking an additional st3-emphasis lever on top of pos-weight-alone has made things worse (exp7 stacked st3-loss-weight, this stacked oversampling) -- consistent enough now to stop pursuing further stacking. Reverting to pos-weight alone (exp6's config) as the standing st3-focused recipe. insufficient_context/hfss_food_marketing (7-38 real examples total) appear to be at or near a hard floor for what loss-reweighting/oversampling can move at this dataset scale -- further gains on them likely need a different approach (more real labeled examples, or in-context few-shot examples in the prompt) rather than more aggressive training-signal tricks on the same ~15-38 examples.

exp10: --peft-method prompt_tuning --num-virtual-tokens 20 --pos-weight, matched epochs=2, split_seed=309780458. Essentially total failure across the board: dev mean_macro_f1=0.004, test=0.000 -- near-zero on every subtask, not just st3. Only 8,192 trainable params (0.0014%% of the model, vs LoRA's default 1.15M/0.19%%) is nowhere near enough capacity to learn this structured-JSON-generation task in 2 epochs/1853 examples -- prompt-tuning is known in the literature to need far more training (often 100+ epochs, or much larger virtual-token counts, or bigger base models) to approach LoRA's quality; this isn't a bug, just an expected mismatch between method and training budget at this scale. Not pursuing further prompt-tuning runs at this budget -- would need a fundamentally larger compute allocation (many more epochs) to get a fair read, which isn't a good trade against this being a low-cost proxy environment. LoRA remains the standing PEFT method.

mini-baseline: microsoft/Phi-4-mini-instruct, --target-modules qkv_proj (Phi3 fuses q/k/v into one matrix, verified via subagent investigation), --sample-size 100 --test-holdout 20 --epochs 1, split_seed=2097561726. Pipeline plumbing confirmed working end-to-end: model loads (no trust_remote_code needed), qkv_proj LoRA target resolves and injects cleanly (2.1M trainable params), chat template renders correctly, generations parse as valid JSON. But dev/test mean_macro_f1=0.000 -- every single prediction (checked submission.jsonl and test_submission.jsonl directly) came back byte-for-byte identical: {"st1":"other","st2":[],"st3":["insufficient_context"]}, regardless of input. This is mode collapse to a constant output from having only 100 train examples for 1 epoch on a totally novel structured-JSON task for this base model -- not a pipeline bug, just too little training to be informative. This scale (100/1 epoch) confirms the pipeline works but is NOT large enough to give a real rough-performance read; would need a bigger --sample-size and/or more epochs for a meaningful mini-baseline number.

mini-baseline: gemma-4-E2B-it-text-only (~4.6B params), --target-modules q_proj,o_proj (verified full 35/35-layer coverage; default q_proj,v_proj would silently only adapt v_proj on 15/35 layers due to num_kv_shared_layers=20 -- 20 layers share k/v from an earlier layer and have no local v_proj module at all). First attempt at --max-length 4096 (script default) OOM'd mid-epoch (step 22/100): gemma's 262144-token vocab is ~1.7x Qwen's, so the batch*seq_len*vocab logits tensor is much larger, and a long training example combined with the full 23GB GPU pushed past capacity. Retried with --max-length 2048 + PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True, succeeded. --sample-size 100 --test-holdout 20 --epochs 1, split_seed=1844212737. Result is striking: dev mean_macro_f1=0.562, test=0.418 -- a real, discriminating signal (not mode collapse) from only 100 training examples / 1 epoch, in the same ballpark as the Qwen3-0.6B track's full-scale (1853-example, multi-epoch) baselines. Plausibly reflects gemma-4-E2B's much larger base model (4.6B vs Qwen's 0.6B, ~8x) being far more sample-efficient at this task. Caveat: n=100 dev / n=20 test is a tiny, high-variance sample (this number should NOT be treated as comparable in precision to the Qwen track's 504-dev/500-test runs) -- promising enough to warrant a proper full-scale run, not yet a confirmed result. Keeping as a positive initial signal.

full-scale gemma-4-E2B: full train (1853) / dev (504), epochs=2, --target-modules q_proj,o_proj, --max-length 2048 (reduced from default 4096 to avoid the OOM seen in the n=100 mini-baseline's first attempt), split_seed=368834301. Near-total collapse: dev/test mean_macro_f1 ~0.004-0.007. CORRECTED diagnosis after direct inspection (an earlier read of this as 'mode collapse to a fixed wrong answer' was wrong): every single prediction is byte-identical to lora_generative.py's hardcoded parse-failure fallback ({"st1":"other","st2":[],"st3":["insufficient_context"]}, which is literally what sanitize_st3([]) returns -- an empty list is falsy in Python). Loaded the trained adapter directly and generated on raw dev examples: the model outputs ONLY '<eos>', zero content tokens, for every input -- true generation collapse, not a wrong-but-coherent answer. Ruled out: (1) truncation -- max_length=2048 gives 461 segment-text tokens, tight (p50 segment is ~1182) but not degenerate/empty; (2) a label-construction bug -- directly inspected GenerativeDataset's built labels for gemma's tokenizer on a real example, supervised span decodes to the exact correct JSON+eos, no issue. Training loss dropped from 0.55 (epoch1) to 0.10 (epoch2) -- low but not NaN/diverging by that metric -- yet dev was ALREADY fully collapsed at the end of epoch 1 (0.003), not something that developed between epochs. This points to genuine training instability from sustained high-LR (2e-4, same as Qwen's tuned default) over ~463 steps/epoch -- the n=100 mini-baseline that worked (dev=0.562) only saw ~25 total steps, never enough exposure to reach whatever step count this collapse sets in around. Next: retry at a much lower --lr to test this directly.

context-sweep 1/4: --context transcript (Level 1 only -- just the transcript text, no video metadata, no product page at all), matched epochs=2, --pos-weight, split_seed=1260877750, otherwise standing recipe. Best dev at epoch 2 = 0.605, test=0.586 -- notably small dev/test gap (0.019, among the smallest seen in this track) and a strong st3 result (dev=0.608/test=0.549, one of the best st3 scores of any experiment so far). Also much cheaper: ~28min total (14:50-15:18) vs ~55-70min for full-context runs -- shorter prompts train and generate() faster. First data point in a --context sweep (transcript/no_product_page/st2_page/full) testing the paper's own accuracy-vs-cost framing (Data Access Levels). Keeping as a genuinely strong, cheap result -- surprising that dropping ALL video/product context doesn't hurt (and may help st3/generalization) relative to full-context runs, though cross-run noise (~0.2 floor) means this needs the other 3 context levels for a fair comparison before drawing conclusions.

context-sweep 1/4 (RE-RUN post leakage-fix, commit 9e8946a): --context transcript --st3-only, matched epochs=2, --pos-weight, split_seed=487509613. st1/st2 columns are n/a (--st3-only mode: st1/st2 are a fixed placeholder, mean_macro_f1 is not meaningful, best-checkpoint selection uses st3_macro_f1). REAL dev st3_macro_f1=0.201 (epoch2), test=0.200 -- extremely close dev/test agreement, a good sign of a clean measurement now. Compare to the PRE-FIX transcript-context row (commit 2595582, this same context level, full st1/st2/st3 completion, not st3-only): that row reported dev st3=0.608/test=0.549 -- roughly 3x higher than this genuine number. This is the leakage bug's actual measured impact on st3 specifically. ALL commit hashes before 9e8946a in this file are known-invalid (see feedback_eval_leakage_bug memory) -- this is the first trustworthy data point in the context sweep.

context-sweep 2/4: --context no_product_page --st3-only, matched epochs=2, --pos-weight, split_seed=207367891. dev st3=0.219 (epoch2)/test=0.196 -- essentially flat vs context-sweep 1/4's transcript-only result (dev=0.201/test=0.200), despite mean input length growing 1666->2157 tokens (+491, adding video title/description/official_disclosure). Adding video metadata doesn't clearly help or hurt st3 at this scale. Consistent so far with the separate data-analysis finding (see project-st3-context-rungs memory) that most st3 labels don't benefit from context beyond the transcript.

context-sweep 3/4: --context st2_page --st3-only, matched epochs=2, --pos-weight, split_seed=1809711824. dev st3=0.224 (epoch2, best of the sweep so far)/test=0.211 (also best test so far), mean input length ~2347 tokens (vs transcript's ~1666, no_product_page's ~2157) -- so filtering the product page down to just its ST2-bearing lines does slightly outperform both transcript-only and no_product_page, a small but consistent step up rather than flat. Still within the ~0.02-0.03 range of the other two sweep points, not a dramatic win, but the only context level so far to beat transcript-only on both dev and test simultaneously.

st1/st2-focused baseline (RE-PRIORITIZED 2026-08-14: user pivoted away from st3 entirely, see feedback-st12-focus memory): --st12-only (new flag, mirror of --st3-only -- completion drops st3 entirely, {"st1":...,"st2":[...]} only), --context full (standing default), matched epochs=2, --pos-weight, split_seed=1378751192. st3/mean_macro_f1 columns n/a (st3 is a fixed placeholder in this mode, not meaningful; best-checkpoint selection used mean(st1,st2)_macro_f1). Best dev at epoch 2: st1=0.618/st2=0.538 (mean=0.578, up from epoch1's 0.565). Test holdout: st1=0.624/st2=0.711 -- both at or above dev, no overfitting red flag, and st2 test notably higher than dev (0.711 vs 0.538) which is a good sign though single-run noise could be part of it. First trustworthy (leakage-fixed) full-context st1/st2 baseline -- next steps: try context ablation (transcript-only etc, mirroring the st3 sweep) and without --pos-weight to see if it's helping or neutral for st1/st2 specifically.

st12-only context ablation: --context transcript (vs full-context baseline above), matched epochs=2, --pos-weight, split_seed=230126473. dev st1=0.570/st2=0.463 (mean=0.517), test st1=0.559/st2=0.485 (mean=0.522) -- both clearly below the full-context baseline (dev mean=0.578, test mean=0.667), unlike the st3 sweep where dropping context barely moved st3_macro_f1. Makes sense: st2 (product category) plausibly depends heavily on the product page/video metadata that transcript-only discards, unlike st3's compliance flags which are mostly transcript-derived. Discarding transcript-only for st1/st2 -- keep full context as the standing recipe for this target; no further context-reduction ablation planned unless a cheaper rung (e.g. no_product_page) is worth checking for a smaller cost/accuracy tradeoff.

st12-only WITHOUT --pos-weight (isolating its effect vs the full-context baseline above, which had --pos-weight on), --context full, matched epochs=2, split_seed=166953285. Best dev at epoch 2: st1=0.713/st2=0.592 (mean=0.652) -- clearly above the pos-weight baseline's dev mean=0.578 (+0.074, epoch1 here already beat pos-weight's epoch2). Test: st1=0.613/st2=0.775 (mean=0.694), also above the pos-weight baseline's test mean=0.667. Initially read as a real pos-weight-hurts-st1/st2 signal and provisionally adopted as the standing recipe -- but see the replicate row directly below, which did NOT reproduce this. Downgrading to discard/inconclusive: this run's strength was likely a favorable split draw, not a real pos-weight effect. Kept in the file as the noise-floor illustration for st12-only, same lesson as the st3-only era's exp5 (see superseded feedback-st3-focus).

st12-only WITHOUT --pos-weight, REPLICATE of the row above on a fresh split_seed=833084525 (same recipe: --context full, matched epochs=2, no --pos-weight) -- the critical reproducibility check for the "pos-weight hurts st1/st2" hypothesis. Does NOT reproduce: dev mean=0.588 (vs the first no-pos-weight run's 0.652, and close to the ORIGINAL pos-weight baseline's dev=0.578); test mean=0.594, actually BELOW the pos-weight baseline's test=0.667. Conclusion: --pos-weight's effect on st1/st2 (like its effect on st3 in the earlier era, see superseded feedback-st3-focus exp6/7/8) is NOT distinguishable from the rotating-holdout noise floor (~0.07-0.15 swings between identical-recipe runs, consistent with the ~0.09-0.22 range established for the full mean_macro_f1 metric). No confident recipe change here -- reverting the standing st12-only recipe to keep --pos-weight ON (matches the rest of the codebase's default, no clear harm or benefit either way). Two single-run pos-weight-off results (0.652, 0.588 dev; 0.694, 0.594 test) bracket the one pos-weight-on result (0.578 dev, 0.667 test) rather than clearly beating it.

row16-5epoch: post-leakage-fix re-run of row 16's recipe (--context transcript, --pos-weight, full st1/st2/st3 completion, standing hyperparams) at epochs 2->5, using the new --final-eval-only flag (added this run, uncommitted at time of run) to skip per-epoch dev generate()/evaluate() on epochs 1-4 -- only epoch 5 is scored/checkpointed. Also switched dev/test-holdout to small 100-instance subsamples (dev: seeded random 100/504 of dev.jsonl; --test-holdout 100 instead of 500) to keep the now-single eval pass cheap. Total runtime ~63min for 5 epochs + final eval on 2253 train instances, vs row 16's ~28min for 2 epochs + per-epoch eval on 1853/500/504 -- per-epoch-eval removal roughly offsets the extra epochs' training cost. IMPORTANT CONTEXT: row 16 (commit 2595582) predates the eval-leakage fix (9e8946a, see feedback-eval-leakage-bug memory) -- its dev=0.605/test=0.586 mean_macro_f1 and st3=0.608/0.549 are inflated (dev/test prompts had the gold answer embedded, model just echoed it), NOT a valid target to compare against. This row is the trustworthy post-fix measurement of the same recipe, not a replication of row 16's number. Result: test mean_macro_f1=0.483 (st1=0.560/st2=0.531/st3=0.357/st3_family=0.491), dev mean_macro_f1=0.439 (st1=0.493/st2=0.452/st3=0.374/st3_family=0.434) -- test slightly above dev (+0.044), no overfitting flag, though n=100 is a small, high-variance sample (do not treat this as precise as the standard 500/504 runs). st3 (0.357-0.374) is well above the matched-context, matched-completion-mode post-fix reference at 2 epochs (row 17, --st3-only, dev=0.201/test=0.200) -- consistent with 5 epochs helping, though row 17 trained st3 alone (all completion tokens on st3) while this row splits capacity across all three tasks, so the two are not a clean ablation of epochs alone. insufficient_context hit dev F1=1.000 (only 1-2 positives in this n=100 subsample, not a meaningful score) and is absent entirely from test's per-label breakdown (zero support in this n=100 test draw) -- both expected artifacts of shrinking holdout to 100 for a label with ~15 total positives dataset-wide, not a real result for that label. Keeping as the first trustworthy, higher-epoch-budget full-completion result on this context level; the --final-eval-only + small-subsample pattern is a reusable way to afford more epochs cheaply for future sweeps.

st12-5epoch: standing st1/st2 baseline recipe (row 20: --st12-only, --context full, --pos-weight) at epochs 2->5, using --final-eval-only + 100-instance dev/test subsamples (same pattern as row 24 -- see project-final-eval-only-flag memory). split fresh per rotating-holdout rule (seed not pinned). st3/mean_macro_f1 columns n/a (st3 is a fixed placeholder in --st12-only mode, not meaningful; best-checkpoint selection used mean(st1,st2)_macro_f1). Total runtime ~104min (2253 train instances, 5 epochs, full context) vs row 20's ~30-40min estimate for 2 epochs on the full 1853/504/500 split with per-epoch eval -- --final-eval-only doesn't make 5 epochs of full-context training cheap, only removes the repeated per-epoch generate() cost; full-context prompts are the dominant cost either way. Result: test mean(st1,st2)=0.754 (st1=0.689/st2=0.818), dev mean(st1,st2)=0.587 (st1=0.596/st2=0.578) -- test clearly above dev (+0.167 gap, one of the largest seen in this track), no overfitting red flag but a bigger dev/test spread than most rows, plausibly n=100's higher variance rather than a real generalization gap. Compare to row 20 (matched recipe, 2 epochs, full 504 dev/500 test): test mean 0.667 (st1=0.624/st2=0.711) -> this row's test mean 0.754 (st1=0.689/st2=0.818), st1 +0.065 and st2 +0.107, both up. Killed after ~30s once the per-step slowdown was clear (no need to run all 5 epochs to confirm a negative result already this unambiguous). CONCLUSION: batch_size=1 remains correct for this pipeline given its highly variable full-context sequence lengths; naive batch-size increases are a net loss without length-bucketed sampling (not implemented) to group similar-length examples together first.
